articles_used.title: Man convicted of starting Palisades fire in Los Angeles
articles_used.summary_raw: The 30-year-old LA resident was convicted of arson leading to wildfires that killed 12 people and destroyed more than 6,800 buildings.
articles_used.full_text:
Homes along Los Angeles' Sunset Boulevard could be seen engulfed in flames during the fires of January 2025
A jury in Los Angeles has found a 30-year-old man guilty of starting one of the most destructive wildfires in California's history.
Jonathan Rinderknecht was convicted of arson after starting the fires that swept through Pacific Palisades and parts of Malibu in January last year, killing 12 people and destroying more than 6,800 buildings in the US state.
The conviction was handed down nearly five months afterdeadlocked jurors led to the judge declaring a mistrial.
Rinderknecht, who had pleaded not guilty, was convicted of two federal charges. He is due to be sentenced on 17 March when he faces between five and 20 years in prison on each charge.
Jonathan Rinderknecht's arrest in October last year
Rinderknecht was found guilty of lighting a fire on 1 January last year which burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up six days later.
One of the charges was for starting the original brush fire, while the other centred on the damage caused when it reignited into a catastrophic blaze.
"We were determined to hold him accountable, and today's guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended," said Bill Essayli, who leads the US Attorney's Office for the Central District of California.
Rinderknecht is a Los Angeles resident and former ride-share delivery driver.
Defence attorney Steve Haney had argued at trial that prosecutors lacked sufficient physical evidence or records to prove their case.
Lawyers for the defendant said they were "disappointed" by the verdict but respected the jury's decision.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who was widely criticised for her handling of the fires, said in a statement that "no verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured".
"So many are still struggling to rebuild," she said. "For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality."
Prosecutors had argued that Rinderknecht was driven by revenge, anger and loneliness because he had nowhere to go for the holiday.
They cited geolocation data from his iPhone, security camera footage that showed his car's location and witness testimony from passengers.
They alleged that Rinderknecht had a "deeply entrenched belief that the wealthy were destroying the world" and in turn purposely started the blaze in the affluent neighbourhood.
The fire was one of several that ignited back-to-back across the LA region in January, which in total left 31 people dead and destroyed 16,000 structures.

articles_used.title: US-Gericht billigt Vergleich von Bayer mit Glyphosat-Klägern
articles_used.summary_raw: Für den Chemiekonzern Bayer könnten die Klagen wegen des Unkraut-Vernichters Roundup in den USA bald der Vergangenheit angehören. Ein US-Gericht hat einen milliardenschweren Vergleich des Konzerns mit Vertretern der Kläger gebilligt.
articles_used.full_text:
Inhalte zeigen von:
Externe Anbieter:
Stand: 21.11.2026 • 04:50 Uhr
Für den Chemiekonzern Bayer könnten die Klagen wegen des Unkraut-Vernichters Roundup in den USA bald der Vergangenheit angehören. Ein US-Gericht hat einen milliardenschweren Vergleich des Konzerns mit Vertretern der Kläger gebilligt.
Ein US-Gericht hat den milliardenschweren Sammelvergleich des Bayer-Konzerns im Streit um mögliche Krebsrisiken des Unkrautvernichters Roundup mit dem Wirkstoff Glyphosat endgültig gebilligt. Richter Timothy Boyer im US-Bundesstaat Missouri genehmigte die Vereinbarung über bis zu 7,25 Milliarden Dollar vollständig. Sie soll Entschädigungen für Zehntausende Betroffene ermöglichen. Der Vergleich sei "fair, vernünftig und angemessen", schrieb Boyer in seiner Entscheidung.
Der im Februar ausgehandelte Vergleich sieht Zahlungen über einen Zeitraum von bis zu 21 Jahren vor. Damit sollen laut Bayer sämtliche Klagen beigelegt werden, bei denen es um geltend gemachte Erkrankungen am Non-Hodgkin-Lymphom (NHL) geht.
17.02.2026
Mit einem Vergleich hat Bayer den Rechtsstreit in den USA über das umstrittene Pestizid Glyphosat beendet.mehr
"Die finale Genehmigung des Gerichts ist ein entscheidender Meilenstein in der mehrgleisigen Strategie des Unternehmens, um sowohl anhängige als auch mögliche künftige Glyphosat-Klagen einzudämmen", betonte Bayer-Chef Bill Anderson nach der Entscheidung. Ein Schuldeingeständnis sei damit nicht verbunden.
Im Juni hatte Bayer einen wegweisenden Glyphosat-Fall vor dem obersten Gericht der USA gewonnen. Infolge des Urteils des US Supreme Court sind Prozesse gegen Bayer im Grunde nicht mehr möglich, in denen Kläger sich auf fehlende Krebswarnungen auf Verpackungen von Unkrautvernichtern stützen wollen.
Bayer hatte den Roundup-Hersteller Monsanto 2018 übernommen und seitdem Milliarden für Rechtsstreitigkeiten ausgegeben. Dessen Pflanzengift Roundup mit dem Wirkstoff Glyphosat wird mittlerweile als "wahrscheinlich krebserregend" eingestuft. Zehntausende Menschen hatten deswegen Klagen eingereicht. Bayer verweist dagegen auf Studien und behördliche Zulassungen, die die Sicherheit des Mittels belegten.

articles_used.summary_raw: Trump's comments came as Russia launched "biggest attacks this year" against Ukraine.

Watch: Trump defends calling Putin a 'friend'
Ukraine's president Volodymyr Zelensky has labelled Vladimir Putin as a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "friend" following their meeting in China this week.
Speaking to CNN, Zelensky said it was up to the US president "how to call Putin" but "for us, he is an enemy... for us, he's a killer".
On the sidelines of a historic trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Putin on Thursday,Trump called Putin his "friend"and said the two leaders have had a "great relationship for many years".
At least nine people were killed in Russian attacks targeting bridges in Kyiv and railway stations on Friday, days after Ukraine badly damaged the Crimean Bridge.
Zelensky calledthe attack the "biggest this year"and said the country suffered civilian deaths and injuries after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones.
Hours after the strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war".
"They (Zelensky and Putin) both want to end it and it's a very good thing I have a relationship," he said on Friday.
Trump also doubled down on his description of the Russian leader as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US.
However Zelensky said despite Trump's stance, he saw Putin as "a killer".
"I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer because he's killing - by the way- he's killing each day and night," he said.
Zelensky also said speaking about Putin like he is a "friend" means "he doesn't feel enough pressure".
The war of words came as Poland said aRussian cruise missile was among three objectsthat violated its airspace early on Friday.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.

Krywyj Rih ist die Heimatstadt des ukrainischen Präsidenten Selenskyj. Nun wurde die Industriestadt erneut mit ballistischen Raketen beschossen. Eine Rakete schlug demnach nahe Wohnhäusern und einem Restaurant ein.
Die russische Armee hat am Abend die südukrainische Industriestadt Krywyj Rih mit ballistischen Raketen beschossen. Dabei seien mindestens zwei Menschen getötet worden, teilte der Militärgouverneur des Gebietes Dnipropetrowsk, Olexander Hanscha, auf Telegram mit.
Es handele sich um eine Sanitäterin und einen siebenjährigen Jungen. Die Zahl der Verletzten stieg auf 21. Eine Rakete schlug demnach im Zentrum nahe Wohnhäusern und einem Restaurant ein. Fotos des Zivilschutzes zeigten ein weitgehend zerstörtes Gebäude. Russische Militärblogger schrieben dagegen von einem Angriff auf eine Pumpstation.
Krywyj Rih, Heimatstadt von Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj, war ein Zentrum von Bergbau und Metallindustrie in der Ukraine. Gehäufte russische Angriffe haben die Industrie aber zum Erliegen gebracht. Russland überzieht das Nachbarland Ukraine seit mehr als viereinhalb Jahren mit einem verheerenden Krieg. articles_used.title: Clojure will affect the way you think about programming (2017)
articles_used.full_text:
I sometimes get asked for recommendations of what programming language to "learn
next". It's great that folks appreciate the fact that being exposed to several
sufficiently different programming languages is an important step on the path
to programming enlightenment. But it's also true that, given limited free time,
the choice of which languages to learn is important. As the famous quote byAlan Perlissays:
In this post I want to explain why I think Clojure is aterrificlanguage for
this task. Whatever your background, it'salmost guaranteedto affect the way you think about
programming. It's a fairly new language (from 2007) that did a good job of
collecting insights and paradigms from many existing languages and organizing
them into a coherent whole. It's chock-full of great ideas. In
other words, theperfect language to expand your brain.
First and foremost, Clojure belongs to the Lisp family of languages, like Common
Lisp, Scheme and Racket. Lisp is one of the oldest and still most important
families of programming languages to be familiar with. Being a Lisp in this case
means several things:
Importantly, Clojure is a verymodernLisp, with tons of libraries for tasks
common in our day and age. It also builds upon important recent research in data
structures, such as efficient persistent vectors, that only appeared in the
1990s or later. I've been dabbling with various Lisps for almost 15 years, and
Clojure is the first Lisp I'd consider using in production.
I want the stress the importance of full Lisp-style macros once again. Lisp's
(and Clojure's) uniform syntax and macros force us to think about theMeta-circular abstraction- there's just no way
around it! We have to think of our code as data, and this has profound
implications. Back in 2005, when I was still a programming neophyte, I faced a
performance challenge for a data-decoding program I was hacking on in Perl.
Having learned some Lisp, I had the insight ofgenerating and evaluating new
Perl code on the fly,
which turned out to be key to the success of that program. I'm confident I could
not have come up with that solution back then without being aware of the "Lisp
way".
The designers of Clojure are extremely pragmatic, building upon decades of
industry experience. I strongly recommend watching someYouTube videos of talksby leading Clojure developers. In
particular, watch a few of the more popular talks by Rich Hickey - Clojure's
original designer. The Alan Perlis quote mentioned above may be his most
popular, but there's another I find at least as insightful:
There's a certain quality in programmers I believe we can all recognize. It can
only come fromreal, hard-won experience of building systems for many years
and pondering about how to build such systems more effectively next time. Rich
Hickey certainly belongs to this quality category - his talks are very
insightful, and this philosophy reigns in the design and implementation of
Clojure, as well as its (friendly and vibrant) community.
Applications that process and extract useful bits of information from large
datasets all look alike in many programming languages, at least to some extent.
What wereallywant in many cases is SQL-like primitives built into our
languages, but this is often challenging (.NET's LINQ is one example of a
successful approach).
Clojure combines pervasive sequence protocols with persistent data structures
and laziness to make this kind of task natural, using only built-in tools.
Here's a realistic example of a function taken from theClojure Appliedbook:
All the functions used here are built-ins, including the->>macro. This
code reads like SQL and it's efficient too. In fact, it can be made somewhat
more efficient and even seamlessly parallelized usingReducers and Transducers.
Theclojure.speclibrary provides a degree
of type-safety for nested data structures. If you've ever written comments like
"this maps strings to lists, where each list element is a map of ...",clojure.specmakes it more formal and verifiable. This is very useful when
working with data, and is another example of where Clojure's pragmatism shines;
the language is dynamic in its core, but when you need static checking - it's
there, optionally (core.typedis another option for a more statically typed
flavor).
Historically, Lisp programmers weren't the biggest proponents of OOP. This
doesn't mean that OOP has absolutely no value in Lisp-y languages, however.
Common Lisp has had CLOS for decades, and Clojure also comes with an array of
OO-like features.
That said, Clojure's flavor of OOP is particularly powerful and tends to
discourage bad practices. Clojure uses "protocols", which are a kind of
interfaces, and encourages thinking in terms of protocols rather than in terms
of classes with inheritance hierarchies, sort of like Go. Add to that an ability
to do truemultiple dispatchand you have a powerful modeling tool at your fingertips.
It wouldn't be a real language of the 2000s without powerful support for
concurrency and parallelism right at the core. Clojure supports this in many
ways, which are interleaved.
First, it's a functional language with persistent data structures. Persistent
data structures are effectively immutable, which makes them very attractive in a
multi-threaded context. Clojure has a great implementation of persistent data
structures even for things like vectors (which are quite challenging to
implement in an efficient manner). This is a bigger deal than may originally
appear. Pure functions are often great in theory but fail in practice due to too
much copying of non-trivial data structures; Clojure's elegant usage of
persistent data structures solves this problem, making pure functions efficient
and thus much more applicable to a wide array of problems.
Second, Clojure doesn't lock itself in the closet of purism and does support
lower-level primitives for concurrency and mutation, where needed. Atoms are
built-in mutable state units with atomic updates.Refs and transactionsgo further, implementing STM.
Third, Clojure comes with a bunch of concurrency tools built in. Promises,
futures and threads leverage the underlying JVM's threading utilities.
Finally, Clojure has a pretty good implementation of Go's CSP in thecore.asyncmodule. It provides two useful things:
Finally, it's important to mention that Clojure is far from being an academic
exercise. It's used in production by several companies, and has strong roots in
the massive Java ecosystem. Clojure's interoperability with Java is seamless -
Java code can be called from Clojure with no special provisions, and all core
Clojure entities are Java objects deep under the hood.
On the client side, Clojurescript has been gaining traction recently as another
language-compiled-to-JS option. It brings the elegance of Clojure to client-side
programming, among with some unique features likecore.asyncfor
callback-free concurrency.
This doesn't mean that you should only consider Clojure as a fit for your next
project. On the contrary, I recommend learning if even if there's little chance
of using it in production any time soon. In fact, this was exactly my situation,
Clojure is a great language to expand your programming horizons; who knows,
maybe in the future you'll find it useful for some real work. If you do, great!
If you don't, learning it will positively affect how you use other programming
languages.

articles_used.title: They were fined $811m for conning detained migrants, but the scams didn't stop
articles_used.summary_raw: How convicted fraudsters made millions from detained immigrants, evaded efforts to shut down their bail business and left migrants behind bars.
articles_used.full_text:
Mildred Juarez was stuck in detention for a month after her friends sent her bail money to Libre Immigration Services
Every morning for a month, Mildred Juarez woke up at five to be the first person in the showers at the immigration centre in Texas where she was being detained. Her friends had paid her bail, and she wanted to look presentable when she was finally released.
But every day, she was told her bond had not been paid.
Juarez was confused. Her friends had wired $2,600 (£1,970) to a bond company, Libre Immigration Services (LIS), that had been recommended by her lawyer. LIS said it would begin "the process of paying her immigration bond". But the next day came, and the day after that, with no release.
What she didn't know was that LIS was owned by a convicted fraudster, who had acquired the assets of another bail company co-founded by two men who also had fraud convictions. These two men were fined $811m in 2024 for scamming their clients.
Their firm, Libre By Nexus,  which was at one point the largest immigration bail company in America, had appeared to shut down after federal regulators caught up with them.
But public records and BBC interviews with clients and former employees reveal a tangle of interconnected operations continued - along with the flow of cash - while leaving immigrants stuck in detention centres.
Since President Donald Trump has returned to office after promising an immigration crackdown, Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has made over 1.2m arrests, and fast-tracked deportations. The administration has tried unsuccessfully to make it illegal to give migrants bail but the sharp increase in detentions has increased demand for bond companies to secure bail and their release.
Conditions in these centres can be poor. Held in custody, away from family, often scared to speak out, many have faced health problems and endured inadequate food or treatment, according to immigrant advocates and reports by the US government.
This video can not be played
"He did everything right" - The impact of Trump's immigration crackdown in Ohio
In the detention centre where Juarez was locked up, she and about 100 other detainees slept in bunks laid out in rows in a cacophonous room. The lights were left on all night and guards routinely woke everyone up for roll call. According to Castro and advocacy groups, detainees who caused trouble were put in "the hold" - solitary confinement.
The White House and officials from Homeland Security did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.
For Juarez, the wait to be bailed out of detention seemed interminable.
In an email to the BBC, a spokesperson for LIS said Juarez "misunderstands" their services - that they are not bondsmen themselves, but they connect detained individuals to those who are licensed bondsmen. They said another company ultimately decided not to work with her.
An email sent by LIS, and reviewed by the BBC, said that the company had paid a cash bond to ICE on behalf of Juarez. The message was forwarded to Juarez as proof of payment a few days before her release.
But it was another bail agent, who was not affiliated with LIS, that got her out of detention - after her friends raised even more money to hire another company.
"I was losing it inside there," Juarez recalled, using an expletive.
"I lost everything. When I was released I had nightmares I was back inside."
Libre Immigration Services never paid back her deposit, despite sending messages promising a refund.  A spokesperson told the BBC that they would refund Juarez's bail amount once her friend verified their details.
It is notoriously difficult for migrants like Juarez to make bail, which can be upwards of $7,000.
Once charged with illegal entry, a judge may grant bail, which allows the migrant to live freely while their case is heard, a process which can take years. Once a person's court case is completed, the bond amount is returned.
Bail agents, who are licensed to provide a down payment on bail and vouch that if the accused does not show up for court they will pay the rest, can help people get out of detention sooner. But many won't help migrants because they view them as too much of a flight risk. A 2024 government report found that a third of migrants not already in custody did not show up for court.
Libre by Nexus, also known as Nexus, was willing to take that risk.
Founded in 2013, its co-founders Michael Donovan and Richard Moore had served prison time in the 1990s and early 2000s for a string of fraud and forgery convictions.
Through his attorney, Donovan declined to comment. Moore did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.
Although people with felony convictions are barred from holding a bond licence in many states, Nexus operated as a kind of middleman between immigrant clients and licensed bondsmen.
Holed up in detention in Louisiana after crossing the border, Rosa Murillo heard about Libre by Nexus from another inmate, and the 18-year-old Honduran's mother called them to arrange her $7,000 bail.
A Nexus employee picked her up and took her to a hotel room where she was told she would have to pay $420 a month and wear a GPS ankle monitor until her case was completed.
Rosa Murillo says she was ashamed to wear the ankle bracelet that Nexus required
Federal regulators accused Nexus of implying, in their contracts, that the GPS bracelets were court-mandated, when they were actually the private company's requirement.
Murillo got a job as a waitress and tried to hide the ankle bracelet for fear that people might think she was a violent criminal.
Over the course of a decade, Libre by Nexus enabled more than 20,000 migrants like Murillo to be released on bail - and took in more than $230m in revenue, court documents show.
But the ankle bracelets were a constant source of annoyance for Nexus clients released from detention, according to two former employees who spoke to the BBC.
A former Nexus co-owner, Evan Ajin, told the BBC that the company stopped requiring released detainees to wear ankle bracelets in 2018.
When Mark Supetran worked for Libre by Nexus, he says he would tell people about how they had to wear an ankle bracelet
But Mark Supetran, who was based in the Philippines and worked for the company for a few months in 2022, says the bracelets were still in use when he worked for the company.
Supetran said he would field 80 calls a day from people who were either going through the process themselves or were the loved one of someone who was. Telling them they would have to wear a tag on release was part of the conversation.
"Part of the script was to say something like: 'The client will be wearing an ankle monitor.' So that got me thinking, like, why?" he recalled. "It doesn't make sense, we're not the government."
Not getting refunds of bail deposits was another complaint. Another former employee told the BBC he was instructed to tell callers that they would get their money back once their case was completed.
"But that that was never the case," he told the BBC. "I mean, you had people calling me in almost every day like 'Hey, am I gonna get my money back? Am I gonna get my money back?'"
Ajin, the former Nexus co-owner, told the BBC that the contract clearly stated that monthly fees did not go towards their bond, but were programme fees, and so they could issue no refund.
The US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), an agency created to stop predatory lending and other abusive financial practices, successfully sued Libre by Nexus and its parent company.
The lawsuit accused the firm of running a "predatory immigrant-services scam" that trapped victims into paying high, long-term fees. Nexus also misrepresented and concealed the terms, the lawsuit alleged, such as the non-refundable, monthly payments.
The judgment sided with the CFPB and a federal judge found the company liable for using predatory tactics against its clients in 2024, fining Nexus, its parent company, Ajin, Donovan and Moore $811m.
In addition to the hefty fine, the judge forbade the company from collecting on past debts.
Days after the 2024 order, Donovan sold a number of the company's assets, including customer lists and records - for $3.50.
As part of the agreement the buyer would also take on its debt.
Ajin says he ceased contact with everyone involved following the sale.
Moore is now in prison, after being convicted of filing fraudulent Nexus taxes. He and Donovan, who is also behind bars, are awaiting sentencing for insurance fraud and conspiracy. Donovan has also been charged with sexually abusing a boy under 12, but has not entered a plea in that case.
The purchaser of Nexus's assets was a Pennsylvania businessman named Vincent Smith, who had been sentenced to 10 months' probation in 2015 for conspiring with employees to write over $2m in fake bail bonds.
Smith called the new business Libre Immigration Services.
This March, the judge who issued the fine also ruled the sale of the company had violated her order by transferring the debts.
Judge Elizabeth Dillon voided the sale, but did not shut Libre Immigration Services down. She is due to review claims that LIS also violated the order by trying to build an app to collect debts from Nexus's old clients.
A former paralegal at Nexus, who went on to work for LIS, told the BBC about the app. She said after the sale, the lines between the two companies were blurred.
Another employee confirmed her account independently to the BBC, noting that the app was never finished because they could not obtain the client data.
A hearing date has not been set, and LIS has denied any wrongdoing, noting the company was never in possession of the client lists.
A screenshot of Libre Immigration Service's website
Libre Immigration Services continues to solicit immigrant clients and advertises its services online and on social media.
Its website features glossy photos of beaming families alongside the promise to "get your loved one released from a detention centre today!".
That wasn't Janie Aviles's experience. She had wired Libre Immigration Services $10,000 to help get her friend out of detention in Texas. But LIS did not pay his bail, Aviles said, until a month later, leaving him, like Juarez, in limbo.
When she called they offered various explanations and then stopped answering the telephone, she said.
Eventually she drove to the office listed on the website, which had shown a picture of LIS's logo hanging above the door. But on arrival, she found there was no storefront with the business's name and logo anywhere.
She said the company finally paid the bail a month after getting the funds, after she had reported them to the district attorney. No charges have been laid.
An LIS spokesperson said that "verification of significant information had to occur to prevent or minimise loss".
"The application was ultimately approved, and the cash bond was pledged to ICE. Presumably any delay related to the substantial bond amount and the heightened requirements of review."
They also said the office at that location was for business operations, and not client services, and that a sign had been ordered and would be installed, pending permits.
But the ordeal was enough to anger Aviles, who feared for her friend while he was stuck in detention.  "I'm like 'This ain't right.'"

articles_used.title: Jugendliche erneut zu Tausenden auf den Straßen
articles_used.summary_raw: Zehntausende junge Menschen haben am Freitag friedlich für die Anliegen ihrer Generation demonstriert. Nach dem Ende der "Gen Z regelt"-Demos gab es mancherorts zwar doch noch Krawalle, eine Eskalation wie an Halloween blieb aber aus.
articles_used.full_text:
Inhalte zeigen von:
Externe Anbieter:
Stand: 21.11.2026 • 03:38 Uhr
Zehntausende junge Menschen haben am Freitag friedlich für die Anliegen ihrer Generation demonstriert. Nach dem Ende der "Gen Z regelt"-Demos gab es mancherorts zwar doch noch Krawalle, eine Eskalation wie an Halloween blieb aber aus.
In vielen deutschen Städten hat es wieder Protestaktionen junger Leute gegeben. Demonstrationen gab es unter anderem in Berlin, Hamburg, Frankfurt am Main, Leipzig, Bremen, Freiburg und Köln. Zu den Kundgebungen aufgerufen hatten mehrere Organisationen und Initiativen, darunter die Bewegung "Gen Z regelt" sowie die Bundesschülerkonferenz.
Laut "Gen Z regelt“ waren diesmal knapp 90.000 Menschen dabei - deutlich weniger als bei den ersten großen Jugendprotesten vor rund drei Wochen. Sie demonstrierten für mehr Geld für Schulen, Suchthilfe und Psychotherapie, ein bezahlbares Leben, mehr Klimaschutz und ein Nein zu eine möglichen Wehrpflicht.
Die Polizei hatte sich vielerorts mit einem Großaufgebot auf mögliche Krawalle vorbereitet. Bis in die frühen Abendstunden blieb es bei oft regnerischem Wetter zunächst weitgehend friedlich. Erst später gab es mancherorts Randale.
In Hamburg warfen Vermummte nach dem Ende einer "Gen Z regelt"-Demo Böller, Eier und Flaschen in Richtung von Polizisten. Mülleimer und Baustellen-Absperrungen landeten auf der Straße und Flaschen gingen zu Bruch. Laut Polizei wurden mehrere Personen in Gewahrsam oder vorläufig festgenommen.
Der Protestzug war zuvor durch die Hamburger Innenstadt gezogen, vom Bahnhof Dammtor zur Sternschanze. In der Spitze waren laut Polizei 4.000 Menschen dabei - etwas weniger als erwartet.
Polizeikräfte kesseln Randalierer im Hamburger Schanzenviertel ein
Nicht nur in Hamburg, auch in Leipzig kam es zu Auseinandersetzungen zwischen Protestierenden und der Polizei. Während des Demozugs mit rund 2.500 Teilnehmern wurde mehrfach Pyrotechnik gezündet, weshalb er vorübergehend gestoppt wurde.
Später seien etliche Teilnehmer in den Süden der Stadt gezogen, teilte die Polizei mit. Dabei seien Beamte mit Feuerwerkskörpern beworfen worden. Die Polizei habe daraufhin Wasserwerfer dorthin verlegt und sie, nachdem es zu weiteren Angriffen auf die Einsatzkräfte gekommen sei, dann auch eingesetzt.
Laut einem Sprecher waren fünf Hundertschaften der Polizei im Einsatz. Ein Polizist sei durch ein Knalltrauma verletzt worden. Mehrere Personen wurden festgesetzt - nach Polizeiangaben wegen des Verdachts, während und nach der Versammlung Straftaten begangen zu haben.
Protestierende zünden Pyrotechnik in Leipzig
Bei der Demonstration gegen Aufrüstung und Wehrpflicht in Stuttgart kam es laut Polizei zu mehr als 20 vorläufigen Festnahmen. Die Betroffenen sollen unter anderem gegen das Vermummungsverbot verstoßen, Polizeibeamte beleidigt oder Widerstand geleistet haben. Die Ermittlungen laufen noch.
In Bremen stoppte die Polizei den Aufzug vorübergehend wegen Pyrotechnik und des Werfens von Farbkugeln. Zuvor waren mehrere mit roter Farbe gefüllte Weihnachtskugeln auf ein Parteibüro der CDU geworfen worden. Teilnehmer hätten zudem versucht, ein Auto in Brand zu setzen. Dabei sei es zu leichten Beschädigungen gekommen.
In Berlin beteiligten sich der Polizei zufolge etwa 4.000 Menschen an einem friedlichen Protestzug von "Gen Z regelt". Die Initiative selbst sprach von bis zu 15.000 Demonstranten. Auch in Städten wie Erfurt, Potsdam und Magdeburg verschafften sich junge Menschen auf der Straße Gehör.

In Frankfurt am Main, wo die Lage nach den Protesten am Halloween-Abend vor drei Wochen eskaliert war und es schwere Krawalle und Plünderungen gab, blieb es diesmal ruhig.
"Die Bilder vom 31. Oktober haben sich nicht wiederholt", bilanzierte der hessische Innenminister Roman Poseck (CDU) nach dem offiziellen Ende der Demos am Abend. Die Polizei sei mit weit über 2.000 Einsatzkräften stark vertreten gewesen.
Bei der Kontrolle einer Personengruppe nach dem Ende der Jugendproteste wurden vier Menschen vorläufig festgenommen. Laut Polizei steht einer von ihnen im Verdacht, an den Ausschreitungen am 31. Oktober in der Stadt beteiligt gewesen zu sein.

articles_used.title: I Don't Trust Visual Recordings Anymore. But One Day I Will Again
articles_used.full_text:
We will have to label our content to prove its authenticity
Hany Farid is a computer science professor at Dartmouth College, in Hanover, N.H.
In March of this year, a flurry of emails and text messages from a half dozen reporters around the world disrupted my quiet Saturday morning. An Iranian news agency had aired a week-oldvideoof what appeared to be a U.S.-made Tomahawk missile hitting a school.News reportsclaimed that the strike killed more than 175 people, most of them children. The U.S. president and military denied responsibility. In the age ofgenerative AIand all thingsdeepfake, everyone—including me—was skeptical of the video’s authenticity.
I get this type of request a lot. For the past three decades, I’ve been developing mathematical and computational techniques toanalyze and detect manipulationindigital media. Over this time, I think it’s fair to say that I, like most people, have approached visual recordings with a “presumption of authenticity”: If a skeptic claims that a recording is fake, the burden of proof is on them.
In today’s world of generative AI, however, I think we need to shift this stance to a “presumption of fake.” That is, the burden is now on the creator to prove that their content is real. While this new stance may seem unfair to legitimate creators, I think it both reflects reality and points to a future where we will once again be able to trust that most online media is what it appears to be.
Even last March, I was already tilting toward a presumption of fake. My initial response to the reporters was something along the lines of, “I am suspicious of the video because the quality is low, it emerged weeks after the bombing, and it is only being distributed by an Iranian news agency with a less-than-stellar record of accurate reporting.”
Given the potential implications—if the video was indeed real, however, I resigned myself to spending my Saturday morning analyzing it.
I first reasoned that if the Tomahawk missile was digitally added to each frame of the video without taking into consideration the camera motion, we might see a physically implausible missile path. So I aligned the video frames using a stationary background landmark as a reference. In the updated video, the missile did, in fact, move in a nearly linear trajectory. (See the yellow dots in the composite shown below.)
I next asked if the size (in pixels) of the missile in the video was plausible. Under some reasonable assumptions, I estimated that the missile in the video corresponded to a 6-meter Tomahawk at a distance of approximately 100 meters. The distance seemed plausible from the scene and was also consistent with the delay of 0.3 seconds from visible impact to the sound of impact, given that sound travels at 343 meters per second.
A composite photo composed of frames from a video of the Tomahawk strike reveals the missile’s trajectory.Hany Farid; Source: Mehr News
Despite the mounting evidence, though, I struggled to refine my answer for the reporters.
My skepticism was fueled by a recentstudyI worked on with colleagues at the University of California, Berkeley, that showed how hard it is to distinguish real from fake videos. Observers are now so suspicious of videos in general that they have trouble convincing themselves that a video is real.
But after a few more hours and a few more analyses with the missile video, I finally decided that it was authentic, and I gave the reporters my updated view.
This analysis marked a turning point for me. I realized I was just like the participants in our study: The lack of artifacts was not enough to readily convince me a video is real. I had flipped from a presumption of real to a presumption of fake.
When the visual record is no longer reliable, what can we do?
The types of forensic analyses that I routinely perform do not currently operate at internet scale and speed. But provenance signals can. These signals include content credentials and watermarks that are inserted or embedded at the time of creation or recording.
Credentials that follow theC2PAstandard, for example, attach a cryptographically signed manifest to a photo or video at the moment of capture; thismetadatarecords the device, the time and location of the recording, and any subsequent edits. Because the manifest is signed, any tampering with either the content or its history can be detected later by machine. Watermarks, likeGoogle’s SynthID, embed an imperceptible signal directly into the pixels or audio samples that identifies the content’s origin.
Apple recentlytook these ideas a step further. On some of its newest iPhones, the camera sensor can cryptographically sign the raw pixel data as it’s captured. That signed data is then developed into areference imagesaved alongside the normal, editable photo. Anyone can then compare the two and see exactly what, if anything, was changed.
These provenance signals are often criticized as being only a partial solution or vulnerable to attack. This is true if we think of them as mechanisms for catching bad actors. But that’s not what they’re supposed to do. Their purpose is to let good actors prove that their audiovisual recording is what it claims to be.
Provenance signals thus need not be adversary-proof. Instead, these signals are part of a new reality in which consumers, journalists, and the courts must adapt to a presumption of fakeness. If enough good actors adopt these mechanisms, they can begin to drown out bad actors. In other words, we have to switch from a model of “catch the bad actors” to “empower the good actors.”
This switch from trust to distrust of digital media has expanded to include routine video calls.
In September 2024, for example, Senator Ben Cardin (D-Md.), then chair of the Foreign Relations Committee, received a video meeting request from Dmytro Kuleba, who until a few weeks earlier had been Ukraine’s foreign minister. During the call, Cardin became suspicious when, out of character, Kuleba pressed him on whether the U.S. should allowUkraineto fire long-range missiles intoRussia. Cardin ended the call. Later, the State Department confirmed that Kuleba had never requested the meeting, and the Senate security office warned staff that foreign adversaries, possibly Russian, would likely try similar faked meetings again.
All it takes to conduct this type of impersonation is a face swap or avatar deepfake, along with voice conversion, both of which substitute the speaker’s face and voice for deepfaked versions in real time. These technologies are readily available in commercial products and open-source libraries and run on nothing more powerful than a modern laptop.
This video illustrates the current state of face-swap deepfakes.
Farid’s Company GetReal Shows How Real Deepfake Videos Look TodayYour browser does not support the video tag.Firms that verify provenance have to move fast to detect real-timedeepfakes.Hany Farid, GetReal
Firms that verify provenance have to move fast to detect real-timedeepfakes.Hany Farid, GetReal
Unlike the Tomahawk video, which I could sit with for a morning analyzing frame by frame, a live video call offers no time for human analysis. On the other hand, real-time deepfakes pose new challenges for their creators: A fake video call has to be generated at around 24 frames per second to fool the eye into perceiving realistic motion. As a result, the deepfake-video-call software has to takeshortcuts, such as simplifying faces and how they interact with their surroundings, and allowing some drift between audio and video or between video frames. The human eye doesn’t notice the shortcuts, but we can forensically expose them.
Provenance signals should eventually play a role here. Video-calling software could apply the same cryptographic signing to each frame of a live video stream that Apple now applies to still photographs. A face swap necessarily occurs between a speaker’s camera and thevideoconferencingsoftware, and so the software could verify in real time whether the frames it’s receiving were signed by a physical camera sensor or whether they were altered in transit. As before, the burden shifts from catching the impersonator to allowing real participants to prove they are who they claim to be.
For the first two decades of the digital revolution, forensic analysis—finding the telltale traces of manipulation—was enough to adjudicate most questions of authenticity. The AI revolution, however, has changed the scale and speed of manipulation beyond whatforensicsalone can handle. To believe a recording is real now, it must also carry a provenance signal from the point of recording. The two approaches work together, with provenance allowing good actors to be trusted, while forensic analyses root out the bad actors.
Hany Faridis a computer science professor at Dartmouth College, in Hanover, N.H. About 10 years ago, he randomly picked up a book in the library on the federal rules of evidence and was astonished to learn that courts made no distinction between photos from negatives and digital photos, even though the latter can be easily altered. “Digital photography was just getting started,” Farid says. “I realized this was really going to be a huge problem.” Since then digital photo forensics has become the focus of his research. He now frequently testifies in U.S. courts and advises law enforcement agencies. “All that from picking up a book,” he says.
The emerging authentication and provenance systems make a lot of sense for mainstream uses. I get the impression we'll still need forensic analysis for plenty of edge cases, though. People using older hardware or anyone trying to capture evidence in situations where it isn't safe to share clues about the media's origin come to mind.

articles_used.title: ANC fights to keep control of South Africa's key cities after election setback
articles_used.summary_raw: The ANC appears reluctant to replicate its national power-sharing deal with the pro-business DA at the local level.
articles_used.full_text:
The ANC got the most votes overall but lost control in more than half of the councils it won in 2021
The party that has dominated South Africa for more than 30 years is in a race against time to secure power-sharing deals in most of the country's cities after a massive drop in its support in this month's local elections.
The African National Congress (ANC) suffered its worst result since it came to power in 1994 when South Africa transitioned from the racist apartheid system to democracy.
It won a majority in just one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo, down from six in the last elections. It won the most votes in just two of the country's eight cities, compared with six in 2021.
At the national level, the ANC is sharing power with its long-time rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA), but while there is still no official announcement, it appears that ANC party officials do not want to replicate this at the local level.
Parties have until 27 November to negotiate and form local governments.
While the ANC saw a massive decline in its support, it still got more votes than any other party, 31%, down from the 46% in the last local election.
But in the country's economic powerhouse, Gauteng province, which includes Johannesburg and Pretoria, the picture is different. The pro-business DA got the most votes in both cities, as well as the province's other main region, Ekurhuleni.
Nationally, the party got 25% of the vote, up from 22% five years ago.
It also retained its majority in its power base of Cape Town, and got the most votes in Nelson Mandela Bay, where Gqeberha (Port Elizabeth) is located.
The left-leaning uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party, led by former President Jacob Zuma, came third, with 10% of the vote. This is a repeat of its performance in the 2024 national election, when it came in third and became the official opposition after the DA joined the coalition government.
It emerged as the biggest party in KwaZulu-Natal province, which includes the port city of Durban, securing 34% of the vote. However, this leaves it reliant on agreeing a coalition with other parties.
The only party to secure an overall majority in a city was the DA in Cape Town.
The DA and ANC have had an uneasy alliance since they entered a coalition, along with eight other political parties, in 2024.
The two, long-standing rivals due to their opposing policies, were forced into an agreement after the ANC lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since the end of apartheid. This became known as the Government of National Unity (GNU).
Despite this, the two parties have continued to disagree on key issues, and both sides have threatened to rip up their power-sharing deal.
Ahead of the local elections, analysts predicted that the two parties could team up at municipal level, mirroring the national arrangement.
ActionSA leader Herman Mashaba (left) and ANC chairperson Gwede Mantashe (right) look set to reach on agreement on co-governing some of South Africa's biggest cities
The ANC seems to have rejected this, with state broadcaster SABC reporting that most of the party's top leaders see an agreement with the DA as a last resort.
Instead, the party has been courting smaller parties to try and form councils in South Africa's cities.
In Gauteng, numerous reports point to an arrangement between the party and the anti-immigrant ActionSA, which emerged as the third largest party in the province with 17%, leaving it as a potential kingmaker.
The DA has also been trying to reach arrangements with smaller parties, and the ANC, but looks set to assume the opposition benches at least in Gauteng.
ActionSA is unlikely to work with the DA as they cannot agree on the mayoral candidates in Johannesburg and Pretoria.
It's too early to tell. Neither the ANC nor DA have spoken publicly about the future of their arrangement on a national level amid the ongoing coalition talks but the ANC's reluctance to partner with the DA in key cities points to continued strain between the two.
While the GNU has remained intact since it was formed in 2024, there have been those in the ANC who have been angered by what they view as the DA's dual role as opposition and partner in the coalition government and have pushed for the arrangement to end.
A party insider told the Daily Maverick on Sunday that a nationwide agreement to work with the DA at municipal level "was overwhelmingly rejected" at a meeting held by ANC members.
While some experts predict that the DA may have to consider its position in the coalition government given the ANC's stance, political analyst Andre Duvenhage told the BBC there was a possibility that "a lot of asymmetrical coalitions" could emerge - parties working together in one area and being in opposition elsewhere.
Another political analyst, Sandile Swana, said that any party wanting to leave the GNU over the failure to secure deals locally would be "[shooting] yourself in the foot".
This is what voters want.
The decline in the ANC's support was seen as being mainly due to high levels of corruption and a loss of confidence in its ability to provide basic services, such as electricity, water and rubbish collection.
While some attribute the increase backing for the DA to its record of competent management in municipalities under its control, some have accused it of neglecting poorer areas and townships.
But the experience of coalition governments over the past 10 years does not inspire much confidence that things will improve.
Half of the country's cities have been governed through power-sharing agreements since 2016 and these types of arrangements have often been viewed as unstable and chaotic.
As agreements collapse and new ones are forged, the delivery of basic services has often been affected.
This has been particularly evident in Gauteng, where governance in all three cities has come under scrutiny in recent years partly because of unstable governments.
Experts agree that even after new arrangements take effect, it will take longer than a five-year term to resolve the issues facing many municipalities, particularly South Africa's biggest city Johannesburg.
"I think if we are really turning the ship around, we are talking about a 10-year period," Duvenhage said.
Swana echoed this, saying it would take a decade to "cleanse and purify" local councils and "reinstate them as "proper municipalities".

articles_used.title: Mamdani announces plan to close New York's Rikers Island jail by 2032
articles_used.summary_raw: Plans to shutter the troubled facility date back to 2019, when the city council first voted to close it but delays arose over where to place inmates.
articles_used.full_text:
Perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, the notorious Rikers Island jail complex earned a variety of nicknames over the years
New York City's official overseeing the closure of the city's most notorious jail hopes a new plan from Mayor Zohran Mamdani will lead to "a moment of transformation" for how people are detained in the largest US city.
Mamdani on Friday unveiled a plan to close the Rikers Island complex by 2032, to build four new jails and drastically reduce the city's detainee population.
Plans to shutter the troubled facility date back to 2019, when the city council first voted to close it by this year. But plans have been delayed over the years in part due to the logistical difficulties over where to place inmates.
Dana Kaplan - who Mamdani appointed as the city's "Close Rikers Czar" told the BBC News channel on Friday that his latest proposal is not just about getting rid of a decrepit facility.
It is also a "generational opportunity" to "build a different type of detention system" and figure out how to detain people more appropriately, she said.
The Rikers Island jail complex is perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, and has earned a variety of nicknames over the years because of its dilapidated conditions, including Gladiator School and Torture Island. The jail has housed a number of high-profile inmates awaiting trial, including Tupac Shakur, DMX and Harvey Weinstein.
It houses more than 6,500 inmates at a given time. Mamdani hopes to reduce that number to 4,100 - a goal that has been met with skepticism by the New York City correction officers' union.
"[B]uilding a new system that puts an arbitrary cap on the City's available jail beds is ill-conceived, irresponsible and jeopardizes the safety of all New Yorkers, including our Officers," NYC Correction Officers' Benevolent Association said in a statement. "The City cannot keep the jail population at around 4,100 without irresponsibly releasing individuals who committed violent felony charges."
Kaplan disagreed.
"It's actually possible to have fewer people in jail in New York City - and that is what we should be planning for," she said.
The jail complex has long faced backlash over staffing shortages, crumbling conditions and inmate deaths in the facility, including nine this year. Legislation required the jail to be shuttered by 2027, but Mamdani blamed lags under former Mayor Eric Adams' administration as well as the Covid pandemic for the delays.
Last year, under Adams, a federal judge removed Rikers from the city's control, appointing an independent outside official to make decisions concerning the facility.
In an 88-page report released on Friday, Mamdani said Rikers was a product of "deteriorating infrastructure" and that officials had a "moral imperative" to close it.
New York City Council must approve the updated timeline, with members, including the city's speaker, indicating they support the plan.
Mamdani's office said the city would open up four new jails - one in Brooklyn by 2029,  two in the Bronx and Queens by 2031 and one in Manhattan by 2032.
The mayor's office argues the new, smaller facilities will provide inmates "access to daylight, fresh air and clean space" leading to better outcomes for detainees. The facilities will be easier for families to access as well, as travel to the remote Rikers can take hours.
Mamdani said his administration would work to reduce the number of people being held in jail across New York City, including by offering alternative programmes to detention for some awaiting trial, by making it easier for families to post bail online and by trying to speed up the pretrial legal process.
He also wants to open up hundreds of beds in therapeutic housing units for prisoners with serious mental health issues.

segments.headline: Selenskyj nennt Putin 'Killer' nach Trumps 'Freundschafts'-Äußerungen
segments.narration: Ein deutliches Wort aus der Ukraine: Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj hat Wladimir Putin als 'Killer' bezeichnet. Das war eine direkte Reaktion auf Donald Trumps Äußerungen, der Putin nach einem Treffen in China seinen 'Freund' nannte und von einer 'großartigen Beziehung seit vielen Jahren' sprach. Selenskyj betonte in einem CNN-Interview, dass Putin für die Ukraine ein Feind und ein Mörder sei, der täglich tötet. Unterdessen gab es erneut russische Angriffe auf die Ukraine. Mindestens neun Menschen starben bei Raketenangriffen auf Brücken in Kiew und Bahnhöfe. In Krywyj Rih, Selenskyjs Heimatstadt, wurden zwei Menschen getötet und 21 verletzt, als eine Rakete nahe Wohnhäusern und einem Restaurant einschlug.
segments.summary_short: Präsident Selenskyj bezeichnete Putin als 'Killer', nachdem Donald Trump ihn als 'Freund' bezeichnet hatte, während neue russische Angriffe in der Ukraine weitere Todesopfer forderten.

segments.headline: Betrugsskandale bei Migrations-Kautionsfirmen in den USA trotz hoher Strafen
segments.narration: Ein Besorgnis erregendes Thema aus den USA: Eine Firma namens Libre Immigration Services wird beschuldigt, Migranten betrogen zu haben, die auf ihre Freilassung aus der Haft warteten. Die neue Firma wurde von einem verurteilten Betrüger übernommen und setzte die fragwürdigen Praktiken einer Vorgängerfirma fort, die bereits mit einer Strafe von 811 Millionen Dollar belegt wurde. Trotz der hohen Geldstrafe im Jahr 2024 durch Bundesbehörden scheinen die Betrugsmaschen weiterzugehen, was Hunderte von Migranten in den USA betrifft.
segments.summary_short: Migrations-Kautionsfirmen in den USA betrügen weiterhin Migranten, die auf ihre Freilassung warten, trotz hoher Strafen gegen frühere, ähnliche Unternehmen.

segments.headline: Jugendliche demonstrieren erneut für ihre Anliegen in Deutschland – mancherorts Krawalle
segments.narration: In Deutschland haben Zehntausende junge Menschen erneut für die Anliegen ihrer Generation demonstriert. Die 'Gen Z regelt'-Demos fanden in vielen Städten statt, darunter Berlin, Hamburg und Leipzig. Gefordert wurden mehr Geld für Schulen, Suchthilfe und Psychotherapie, ein bezahlbares Leben, mehr Klimaschutz und ein Nein zu einer möglichen Wehrpflicht. Obwohl die Proteste größtenteils friedlich verliefen, kam es in Hamburg und Leipzig zu vereinzelten Krawallen mit Böllern und Flaschenwürfen. Eine Eskalation wie an Halloween blieb aber aus, da die Polizei mit einem Großaufgebot präsent war.
segments.summary_short: Zehntausende Jugendliche demonstrierten in Deutschland friedlich für ihre Anliegen, doch kam es in einigen Städten zu Krawallen.

segments.headline: ANC kämpft nach Wahlniederlage um Kontrolle wichtiger Städte in Südafrika
segments.narration: Blicken wir nach Südafrika: Der Afrikanische Nationalkongress, kurz ANC, kämpft nach schweren Verlusten bei den Kommunalwahlen darum, die Kontrolle in den meisten Städten des Landes zu behalten. Die Partei, die Südafrika seit über 30 Jahren dominiert, erzielte ihr schlechtestes Ergebnis seit 1994. Zwar erhielt der ANC landesweit die meisten Stimmen, verlor aber die Mehrheit in mehr als der Hälfte der Räte, die er 2021 gewonnen hatte. Nun bleiben den Parteien nur noch wenige Tage, um Koalitionen zu bilden und lokale Regierungen zu etablieren.
segments.summary_short: Der südafrikanische ANC kämpft nach massiven Verlusten bei den Kommunalwahlen darum, in wichtigen Städten Koalitionen zu bilden und die Macht zu erhalten.

segments.headline: New Yorks Bürgermeister Mamdani kündigt Schließung von Rikers Island bis 2032 an
segments.narration: Und zum Schluss noch ein Blick nach New York: Bürgermeister Zohran Mamdani hat einen Plan vorgestellt, die berüchtigte Haftanstalt Rikers Island bis 2032 zu schließen. Stattdessen sollen vier neue, kleinere Gefängnisse gebaut und die Zahl der Häftlinge drastisch reduziert werden. Dieser Schritt wird von Dana Kaplan, der vom Bürgermeister ernannten 'Close Rikers Czar', als 'Chance für einen Wandel' im Umgang mit Inhaftierten in der größten US-Stadt bezeichnet.
segments.summary_short: New Yorks Bürgermeister Mamdani hat einen Plan zur Schließung des Rikers Island Gefängnisses bis 2032 vorgestellt, der den Bau von vier neuen Haftanstalten und eine Reduzierung der Häftlingszahlen vorsieht.
